claim.pdf_says: 14.9.10.4   General rules  — printed in the same bold subsection style and at the same depth as 14.9.10.1 General, 14.9.10.2 General formats and 14.9.10.3 Syntax rules on page 635.
claim.why_it_matters: A fourth-level subsection is emitted at heading level 2, the same level as its own parent '## 14.9.10 DELETE statement' and as '## 14.9.11 DISPLAY statement'. Its three siblings on page 635 are correctly at level 3 (### 14.9.10.1/.2/.3). Any tool that navigates by heading level — the doc index, a TOC generator, or a section-slicing spec lookup — will treat the DELETE General rules as a peer of the statement itself and detach them from 14.9.10, silently truncating what a '14.9.10 DELETE statement' section fetch returns.

verdict.reasoning: Independently confirmed by rendering both pages at 300 dpi. Page 636 (printed folio 606) prints a single bold run-in heading '14.9.10.4   General rules' above 'FORMAT 1' and rules 1)-7); page 635 (folio 605) prints '14.9.10   DELETE statement', '14.9.10.1   General', '14.9.10.2   General formats' and '14.9.10.3   Syntax rules' in the identical bold face, size and left margin. ISO's run-in style does not itself encode depth — the dotted section number does — and 14.9.10.4 is unambiguously a child of 14.9.10. The markdown contradicts that: `rg '^#+ 14\.9\.10' specs/ISO_COBOL.md` returns `## 14.9.10 DELETE statement` (26311), `### 14.9.10.1` (26314), `### 14.9.10.2` (26319), `### 14.9.10.3` (26344), and `## 14.9.10.4 General rules` (26365). The .4 subsection is encoded one level shallower than its own three siblings and at the same level as its parent. No rejection ground applies: the heading text is present and correctly spelled, so this is not a reflow or a misquote; it is not page-break furniture (the running header `# ISO/IEC 1989:2023 (E)` and the `## Page 636` marker are separate lines, both correctly emitted); and it is not cosmetic formatting, because heading level in markdown IS the transcription's encoding of document hierarchy — the encoded parent/child relation is factually wrong relative to the PDF. Normative prose is intact: all of FORMAT 1 rules 1)-7)a)1. on this page transcribe faithfully, so nothing is lost, only mis-nested. Three inaccuracies in how the claim is stated, none fatal: (1) the `kind` label 'missing-heading' is wrong — the heading is present, its LEVEL is wrong; (2) the cited line 26362 is off by three — 26362 is the running header `# ISO/IEC 1989:2023 (E)`, the anchor is at 26364 and the heading at 26365; (3) the impact is overstated for this repo's own tooling — scripts/spec/extract_rule_catalog.py was deliberately hardened for exactly this, its comment reading 'A numbered section heading, e.g. "## 8.4.3.13.3 Syntax rules" or "### 14.9.28.4 General rules"', so that consumer already tolerates both levels; the hazard is real for any NEW level-based navigator but is not currently truncating the rule catalog. Finally, this is not an isolated defect but one instance of a systematic transcription pattern: 162 four-component headings are emitted at `##` against 620 correctly at `###`, and the very next statement's 14.9.11.4 General rules (line 26541) has the same defect — and it is NOT page-start correlated (26541 follows syntax rule text at 26538), so a repair must sweep on the numbering shape, not on page boundaries.
verdict.corrected_description: Wrong heading LEVEL, not a missing heading. specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 26365 emits `## 14.9.10.4 General rules` (anchor `` at 26364) at markdown level 2, while its siblings `### 14.9.10.1 General` (26314), `### 14.9.10.2 General formats` (26319) and `### 14.9.10.3 Syntax rules` (26344) are at level 3 and its parent `## 14.9.10 DELETE statement` (26311) is at level 2. The PDF prints 14.9.10.4 as a normal fourth-level subsection of 14.9.10; the transcription encodes it as a peer of the DELETE statement itself. No normative text is lost — the FORMAT 1 general rules on page 636 transcribe faithfully. Reclassify kind as `heading-level` and correct the cited line from 26362 to 26365. Repair as a PATTERN, not a one-off: 162 headings with four dotted components sit at `##` versus 620 at `###`, including 14.9.11.4 at line 26541, which is mid-page and therefore rules out page-break furniture as the sole cause. Note when scoping the fix that scripts/spec/extract_rule_catalog.py already accepts both levels by design, so the rule catalog is not currently truncated by this; the exposure is to any future heading-level-based navigator or TOC generator.
